subject: Mechanical Engineering
title: Impact Testing: Charpy and Izod
description: A 60-second lesson on Impact Testing: Charpy and Izod.

hook.text: A heavy pendulum swings down and smashes through a notched bar. The energy it loses tells you how tough the material is.

buildup.text: The Charpy test lays the bar horizontally. The Izod test clamps it vertically. Both measure energy absorbed during fracture.

discovery.text: Tough materials absorb a lot of energy — the pendulum barely swings past the break. Brittle materials absorb almost none.

twist.text: Run the test at different temperatures and you find the ductile-to-brittle transition. It's vital for Arctic and cryogenic use.

climax.text: The Liberty ships of World War II cracked apart in cold seas. Charpy testing of hull steel became mandatory afterward.

punchline.text: Smash it. Measure what's left. Know if it can take a hit.

quiz.question: Why did Charpy testing become mandatory for ship hull steel?
options: It measures the steel's resistance to salt water corrosion
Liberty ships cracked in cold seas, revealing the need to test for brittle transition temperatures
It verifies that the hull is thick enough to withstand wave impacts
